source: Inspired by ASA rulings on undisclosed influencer promotion and detox/cure claims

campaign.title: SlimTea 14-day detox — influencer push
campaign.text: Instagram and TikTok posts by fitness influencer @LenaFitLife (280k followers, paid 4,000 EUR per post, contract requires 'authentic tone, no ad markers'). Copy: 'Girls, this little tea has CHANGED MY LIFE. The SlimTea 14-day detox flushes out toxins, melts belly fat while you sleep and cures bloating for good — I lost 6kg without changing anything else! Use my code LENA20.' No #ad or paid-partnership label anywhere. Landing page repeats the fat-melting and cure claims with before/after photos.

source: Inspired by CPC sweep findings and ASA rulings on fake countdown timers and scarcity

campaign.title: FlashSale mattress countdown
campaign.text: Own-brand webshop promotion for the CloudRest mattress. Every product page shows a red banner: 'HURRY — sale ends in 02:59:41' with a live countdown, and 'Only 3 left in stock!'. The countdown resets to three hours whenever it reaches zero or the visitor returns, and stock is not actually limited (fulfilment is made-to-order with 2,000+ units weekly capacity). Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.

source: Inspired by ASA rulings on crypto/investment ads with guaranteed-return claims and fabricated endorsements

campaign.title: CryptoMasterclass — guaranteed returns funnel
campaign.text: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll ads for a 499 EUR crypto trading course: 'Turn 250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days — our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed. Join 50,000 students.' Landing page shows testimonials with stock photos and names we invented ('Marta from Sevilla made 14,000 EUR in her first month') and a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course. Fine print says results may vary.

source: Inspired by UCPD Annex I point 28 enforcement on advertising to children and DSA minor-protection duties

campaign.title: RoboPets launch — kids YouTube push
campaign.text: Campaign for the RoboPets collectible toy line on YouTube Kids channels and a Roblox branded world. Video scripts (voiced by a popular kids' animator): 'The new RoboPets are here! They're SO cool — tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW before your friends get theirs! Ask them today, don't wait!' The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players: 'Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!'

source: Inspired by CPC sweep on subscription traps and misuse of 'free' (UCPD Annex I point 20)

campaign.title: FitCoach FREE trial funnel
campaign.text: Display and social ads: 'Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE — just cover 1.95 EUR shipping for your welcome kit.' Checkout requires full card details; page 3 of the terms states enrolment in a 49.99 EUR/month subscription that starts after 5 days unless cancelled. Cancellation is only possible by phone during business hours, and the retention script requires agents to offer three counter-offers before processing. 'FREE' appears 11 times on the landing page; the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link.

source: Inspired by EC/CPC green-claims actions and ASA rulings on unsubstantiated carbon-neutral claims

campaign.title: FlyGreen — carbon neutral flights
campaign.text: Airline brand campaign across OOH, social and in-app banners: 'Fly 100% CARBON NEUTRAL. Every FlyGreen ticket is climate-positive — you fly, the planet wins.' The claim rests entirely on purchasing unverified forestry offsets covering an estimated 8% of per-flight emissions; no lifecycle data, no methodology page, no third-party verification. The green leaf logo and 'planet-positive' tagline appear on all fares including long-haul.

source: Inspired by DPA enforcement on purchased marketing lists and lookalike audiences without lawful basis

campaign.title: HomeSecure winter blitz — purchased list
campaign.text: Email campaign for home alarm systems sent to 400,000 addresses purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available). The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences. Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') and the privacy policy is not referenced. Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.

source: Inspired by UCPD Annex I point 31 enforcement on false prize notifications

campaign.title: You've WON — iPhone giveaway retargeting
campaign.text: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your number was selected — you've WON an iPhone 16 Pro! Claim within 15 minutes: just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping.' Every visitor 'wins'; there is no draw and no phones are stocked. Paying enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page. A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'.

source: Adapted from Mathur et al. dark-patterns dataset: confirmshaming + hidden costs on a marketplace

campaign.title: StyleHub marketplace checkout optimisation
campaign.text: UX copy changes for our fashion marketplace platform (third-party sellers, EU-wide). The newsletter opt-out link now reads 'No thanks, I hate saving money'. Declining purchase protection shows 'I'll risk losing my order' as the only decline label. A pre-ticked 2.99 EUR 'carbon protection fee' and a 4.90 EUR 'service fee' are added at the final payment step only, not shown on product or cart pages. A/B test shows +18% attach rate.

source: Adapted from dark-patterns dataset: fabricated activity/social-proof messages

campaign.title: TravelNest urgency messaging rollout
campaign.text: Hotel booking site feature: every listing shows rotating messages — '17 people are looking at this hotel right now', 'Booked 43 times in the last 24 hours', 'In high demand!'. The numbers are generated by a random-number function unrelated to real traffic (range tuned by conversion team). The same fabricated counters feed 'Only 1 room left at this price!' banners.

source: Adapted from climatebert/environmental_claims dataset style: vague, unsubstantiated eco claims

campaign.title: EarthWear conscious collection
campaign.text: Fast-fashion capsule launch: 'Our new Conscious Collection is eco-friendly, planet-kind and made with 100% sustainable materials. Shop guilt-free — fashion that loves the Earth back.' The collection is 12% recycled polyester and 88% conventional polyester; no certification, no comparison baseline, no environmental report. 'Sustainable' is not defined anywhere on the site. Green hangtags and leaf iconography across all touchpoints.

source: Adapted from UW Bad Ads dataset: clickbait native advertorials with cure claims

campaign.title: JointFlex native content push
campaign.text: Native advertising campaign on news-site content-recommendation widgets. Headlines: 'Doctors HATE this simple trick — grandmother, 67, cures joint pain in 3 days', 'The pharma industry doesn't want you to know this'. Clicking leads to a fake news article styled like the host newspaper (same fonts and logo placement) that is actually a JointFlex supplement sales page with a fabricated interview of a 'Dr. med. Weber'. No 'advertisement' label on the widget or the article.

source: Adapted from CPC sweep on fake reviews (UCPD Annex I points 23b/23c)

campaign.title: KitchenPro launch review programme
campaign.text: Marketplace launch plan for a blender: buy 300 five-star reviews from a review farm before launch week ('aged accounts, verified-purchase badge included'), and email real customers offering a 20 EUR voucher only if they leave a 5-star review (4 stars or below: no voucher). Product page will display 'Rated 4.9/5 by verified buyers' and a 'Customers' Choice' badge we designed ourselves. Negative reviews are reported for removal as 'spam' regardless of content.

source: Adapted from ASA rulings on beauty filters plus AI Act synthetic-content transparency

campaign.title: LumaSkin serum — AI visuals
campaign.text: Cosmetics campaign for an anti-ageing serum. All 'results' imagery is generated with our image model from a single base photo: wrinkles removed, skin texture synthesised, before/after pairs fabricated. Social clips use an AI-smoothing filter on the presenter while she says 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'. No AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere. Claim on pack-shot overlay: 'Clinically proven -71% wrinkles' (internal survey of 12 employees, no clinical study).

source: Synthetic compliant control: honest promotion, disclosed partnership, truthful discount

campaign.title: AquaPure filter spring promotion
campaign.text: Spring promotion for the AquaPure water filter. Messaging: 'Save 20% until 30 April — regular price 79 EUR, promo price 63.20 EUR' (the regular price has applied since January; the promotion genuinely ends 30 April). Product claims limited to certified facts: 'Removes 99% of chlorine (certified to EN 17093)'. Influencer posts are labelled 'Paid partnership with AquaPure' plus #ad in the first line. No urgency mechanics, no data collection beyond standard web analytics disclosed in the privacy notice, opt-in newsletter with one-click unsubscribe.

source: Synthetic compliant control: GDPR-clean personalised email programme

campaign.title: BookNook member newsletter revamp
campaign.text: Monthly newsletter for bookshop loyalty members who gave specific opt-in consent at signup (unticked box, plain-language notice, consent records kept). Personalisation is limited to genre preferences the member selected in their profile. Every email carries a one-click unsubscribe honoured immediately, a link to the preference centre and to the privacy notice naming the processor. Members who do not open six consecutive emails are automatically suppressed. Copy promotes new titles with accurate prices; no discounts are claimed that were not real.

source: Synthetic near-miss: urgency wording that is factually true and verifiable

campaign.title: Atelier 200 numbered edition
campaign.text: Launch of a numbered limited edition of 200 hand-made watches. Messaging: 'Only 200 will ever be made — each engraved with its number. Pre-orders close Friday 20:00 CET or when the 200 pieces are allocated, whichever comes first.' Production is genuinely capped at 200 (published attestation from the manufacturer), the live counter reflects actual remaining allocations from the order system, and the deadline is real: the configurator goes offline Friday 20:00. No countdown resets, no fabricated demand messages.

source: Synthetic: AI chatbot posing as a human agent, plus undisclosed data reuse

campaign.title: Emma — conversational sales assistant
campaign.text: Website chat widget for a telecom operator. The assistant introduces itself as 'Hi, I'm Emma from the sales team 😊 how can I help?' — Emma is an LLM-driven bot, and the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office'). The bot collects name, email and current provider 'to check offers', and these are stored for follow-up marketing calls; the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use. Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse.

source: Synthetic: undisclosed deepfake celebrity endorsement for a supplement

campaign.title: VitaBoost — Dr. Silva video series
campaign.text: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva, a well-known TV physician who has no relationship with the brand. In the synthetic clips 'he' says: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.' The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional; comments calling them fake are deleted. Media plan: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics.

source: Synthetic: behavioural ad targeting of minors on a platform, quiz-based data collection

campaign.title: VoltZ energy drink — teen engagement loop
campaign.text: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform. A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience. The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00. An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
